issues.legal_issue: Different penalties imposed on employees involved in the same incident do not justify judicial interference with a disciplinary penalty when their charges or responsibilities materially differ and the penalty is not otherwise unlawful or shockingly disproportionate.
material_facts: A joint disciplinary inquiry found misconduct by an officer and two subordinate employees in connection with unlawful grants of occupancy rights over government land.

The officer was charged with granting the rights without following the prescribed procedure and with an ulterior motive; the subordinates faced different charges concerning preparation of a survey map and statements on oath.
The officer held the authority and responsibility to grant occupancy rights, while the other employees were his subordinates.
The officer's removal from service was upheld on departmental appeal, while the co-delinquents received different, lesser penalties on their appeals.

The Tribunal ordered reconsideration on the ground that the officer had been treated differently, but the Supreme Court found the charges and responsibilities were not substantially alike and the removal penalty was commensurate with the proved misconduct.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal was not justified in interfering with the removal penalty merely because the co-delinquents received lesser penalties. The appeal was allowed, and the Tribunal's and High Court's orders were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles stated in B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India, Director General, RPF v. Ch. Sai Babu, Chairman and Managing Director, United Commercial Bank v. P.C. Kakkar, Union of India v. S.S. Ahluwalia, and State of Meghalaya v. Mecken Singh N. Marak, judicial review of a disciplinary penalty is limited: a court or tribunal ordinarily cannot substitute its view of the appropriate penalty and may interfere where the decision is unlawful, materially procedurally irregular, or the penalty shocks its conscience. Relevant considerations include the gravity of misconduct, the employee's duties and responsibility, past conduct and penalties, and the discipline required. A co-delinquent's lesser punishment alone does not warrant interference where charges or responsibilities differ; Balbir Chand v. Food Corporation of India is cited on that point. Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. Ltd. v. Jitendra Pd. Singh and State of U.P. v. Raj Pal Singh do not require equal penalties where the charges are not identical or substantially similar. The disciplinary proceedings here were initiated under Rule 14 of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, for alleged misconduct under Rule 3 of the Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964, concerning duties prescribed by the Dadra and Nagar Haveli Land Reforms Regulation, 1971.

rule.if: disciplinary_penalty_judicial_review and joint_inquiry_with_co_delinquents and co_delinquents_received_lesser_or_different_penalties and (charges_differ or responsibilities_differ) and not penalty_shocks_conscience and not material_procedural_irregularity

predicates.disciplinary_penalty_judicial_review: A court or tribunal reviewed a penalty imposed after disciplinary proceedings.
predicates.joint_inquiry_with_co_delinquents: The employee and other employees were investigated together in a disciplinary inquiry concerning the same incident.
predicates.co_delinquents_received_lesser_or_differ: The other employees received penalties different from, and less severe than, the employee's penalty.
predicates.charges_differ: The misconduct alleged against the employee differed materially from the misconduct alleged against the other employees.
predicates.responsibilities_differ: The employee held duties or authority materially different from those held by the other employees.
predicates.penalty_shocks_conscience: The penalty imposed on the employee was so disproportionate that it shocked the conscience of the reviewing court or tribunal.
predicates.material_procedural_irregularity: A material procedural irregularity occurred in the disciplinary decision-making process.

issues.definition: When a disciplinary penalty is under judicial review, different outcomes for co-delinquents do not alone justify interference if their charges or responsibilities differ and the penalty neither shocks the conscience nor results from a material procedural irregularity.
